title: POC scoping - Cost model & benchmarking - Horizon Analytics
summary: Initial POC scoping focused on unit economics for a 4-week pilot: workload sizing, per-token estimates, batching/caching knobs, target SLOs and budget. Agreed to run benchmarks (latency, p99, cost) with a 2k-user simulated workload and deliver a cost model spreadsheet.
next_steps: Redwood: share benchmark test plan and pricing spreadsheet by 2025-07-11
Horizon: provide sample workload traces & 3 representative prompts by 2025-07-10
Schedule 30m kick-off for benchmark run week of 2025-07-14
action_items: Sofia Chen: Send pricing spreadsheet + benchmark plan (due 2025-07-11)
Maria Gomez: Upload sample production traces and prompt set (due 2025-07-10)
Liam Patel: Prepare dedicated test harness and run first smoke benchmarks (due 2025-07-16)
transcript:
[00:00] Sofia Chen: Hey everyone thanks for joining, we're here to scope the POC for cost modeling and benchmarks with Horizon Analytics, can everyone hear me?
[00:05] Maria Gomez: Yep, loud and clear. Thanks Sofia.
[00:08] Daniel Park: Hi all.
[00:12] Sofia Chen: Cool, quick intros - I'm Sofia, AE at Redwood, and Liam is our SE.
[00:16] Liam Patel: hi all.
[00:20] Ravi Iyer: Ravi here, ML engineer.
[00:22] Sofia Chen: Great. Maria, could you remind us of the main success criteria for the POC?
[00:30] Maria Gomez: Sure. We want to validate two things: (1) that latency fits our interactive UI requirements - p95 under 400ms ideally, or p99 under 700ms as a hard limit; and (2) that per-user monthly cost stays within our budget, which is about $10k a month initially for the feature. Also we need security verification - SOC 2 and enterprise kYes SSO/SAML — sorry, KMS integrations for keys.
[00:50] Daniel Park: and for the timeline we were thinking a 4 week POC with an initial 2 week benchmarking window.
[00:57] Sofia Chen: That sounds reasonable. For the cost side, quick clarification on workload: how many concurrent users and tokens per request are we seeing?
[01:06] Maria Gomez: Our UI does short summarizations and a follow-up Q&A. Average prompt length 60 tokens, generation about 140 tokens per response. Peak concurrent users around 80 during internal testing, production target maybe 200 RPS but ramp. For the POC let's simulate 50-60 RPS sustained with bursts to 120.
[01:28] Ravi Iyer: Also we have a lot of repeated prefixes - users pass the same document content for many prompts, so KV cache or prefix caching could be big.
[01:36] Liam Patel: good to know — cache will reduce compute for subsequent tokens. We'll model both cold and warm cache.
[01:40] Sofia Chen: On unit economics, rough hosted estimates: for the model families you mentioned, generation costs are around $0.0008 per generated token on our baseline open model in hosted mode; with batching and quantization we often see effective per-token drop to $0.00035. Embeddings are different - around $0.00012 per vector call in hosted. These are ballpark for planning — we'll run benchmarks to get precise numbers.
[02:05] Maria Gomez: okay that's helpful. Does that include KV cache benefits or is that raw decode cost?
[02:10] Liam Patel: those are raw decode cost numbers. With KV cache and prefix reuse you're amortizing the context cost — effectively fewer decoder steps per request, so per-request cost can drop 20-60% depending on reuse. Also batching at 16-32 seqs often reduces per-token slew because of kernel efficiency.
[02:26] Daniel Park: can you explain how batching interacts with latency? We're sensitive to p95.
[02:30] Liam Patel: sure. Batching increases throughput efficiency but adds queuing latency. Our runtime supports dynamic batching; you can set a max batch wait (e.g., 5-15ms). For your latency SLOs, we recommend small max batch windows (5ms) and target batch sizes around 8-12 for steady load. That usually keeps p95 low while still giving batching benefit. If you need p99 under 700ms, we can use prioritized routing — reserved slots for interactive requests.
[02:55] Maria Gomez: what about Dedicated vs Hosted? We want deterministic costs.
[02:59] Sofia Chen: Dedicated capacity gives more predictable unit economics — you reserve GPU capacity and you get lower per-token unit cost in exchange for committed spend. Hosted is easier to start with and faster time-to-value. For a POC we often run hosted benchmarking first and then model Dedicated numbers if you want to forecast a monthly committed spend.
[03:18] Ravi Iyer: how much data egress / logging and audit would add? We need audit logs and compliance.
[03:23] Liam Patel: audit logs are additional but usually modest. For Private deployments we integrate with your KMS/HSM and all telemetry can be routed into your SIEM. We'll include audit log sizing in the pricing sheet.
[03:32] Maria Gomez: great. For the benchmark plan what do you normally run?
[03:35] Liam Patel: we'll run a 3-phase benchmark: (1) smoke tests at low qps to sanity-check; (2) scale ramp to target RPS with realistic prompt distribution and cold start + warm cache scenarios; (3) long-run 1-2 hour soak to capture p99 and failure modes. We'll capture p50/p95/p99, tokens consumed, GPU utilization, and cost per 1M tokens. We'll also run an embedding/semantic search benchmark if you plan to use embeddings.
[03:58] Daniel Park: for our team, the most useful number is cost per MAU for the feature. Can you map tokens->MAU?
[04:05] Sofia Chen: yes — we can produce a cost model: inputs are avg tokens per interaction, interactions per MAU per month, and cache-hit rates. We'll create a spreadsheet with knobs: batch size, cache hit %, quantization profile, and both hosted and dedicated unit costs.
[04:18] Maria Gomez: do you have example quantization savings numbers?
[04:21] Liam Patel: with int8 quant we often get ~1.8-2x throughput improvement and maybe 20-35% lower cost compared to FP16 serving, but that depends on model and accuracy tolerance. We'll include recommended profiles based on your eval set.
[04:34] Ravi Iyer: accuracy matters; we'll need to run quality regressions as part of the POC.
[04:38] Sofia Chen: absolutely - we'll tie quality metrics to the benchmark: BLEU/ROUGE isn't always right for these UX cases, so we'll use the prompt set and human eval or automatic heuristics you prefer. If quality regresses beyond an agreed threshold, we halt quantized config.
[04:52] Maria Gomez: timeline? You mentioned a 4-week POC earlier. Can you break that down?
[04:56] Sofia Chen: Proposed timeline: Week 0 (this week) - agreement and data share; Week 1 - Redwood sets up test harness and runs smoke tests; Week 2 - run scale and soak benchmarks; Week 3 - analyze results and run follow-up targeted runs (e.g., different quantization profiles); Week 4 - finish report, cost model, and exec review. We can compress to 3 weeks if Horizon provides prompt set and traces immediately.
[05:18] Daniel Park: budget allocation — you said hosted baseline numbers earlier, if we project 100k user interactions per month at avg 200 tokens total per interaction, what rough monthly spend would that be?
[05:28] Sofia Chen: quick math: 100k interactions x 200 tokens = 20M tokens. At baseline hosted $0.0008/gen-token that's $16k; with batching and caching and quantization optimizations to $0.00035 effective, that's about $7k. So the range is ~$7k-$16k depending on optimizations. That's why the POC is helpful.
[05:46] Maria Gomez: good — that brackets our $10k target.
[05:49] Ravi Iyer: can you run the benchmark against our internal env or only Redwood infra?
[05:53] Liam Patel: we can run both. For deterministic latency we can do a Dedicated trial in Redwood infra or run Private in your VPC if you prefer. For initial cost model we typically use hosted runs plus a simulated Dedicated pricing line. If you want on-prem we can send a small deployable test package.
[06:10] Sofia Chen: risks/unknowns to call out: model variant selection (some open models cost more to run), accuracy vs quantization tradeoffs, and real-world cache hit rates which are dataset dependent. We'll parameterize these in the spreadsheet.
[06:22] Maria Gomez: what about throttling and fallbacks? If capacity is constrained we need graceful degradation.
[06:27] Liam Patel: Redwood supports smart routing and automatic fallbacks to a cheaper model variant — you can set policies by latency/cost. We'll work with you on policy defaults for the POC.
[06:37] Daniel Park: ok. Are there any compliance docs we need to review for the security team?
[06:41] Sofia Chen: yes — we'll share SOC 2 summary, our data flow diagram, SAML/SSO integration notes, and the KMS/HSM whitepaper. Expect those in the packet Sofia will send.
[06:50] Maria Gomez: perfect. One last question — how do you handle tokenization differences? Our prompt includes large doc text.
[06:56] Liam Patel: we'll include tokenizer counts in the benchmark — we can either run with your tokenizer configuration or ours (we typically use standard byte-pair inferences). We'll measure tokens-per-doc to make cost mapping realistic.
[07:06] Sofia Chen: recap and next steps: Redwood to send benchmark plan + pricing spreadsheet by Friday (2025-07-11). Horizon to share sample traces & prompt set by Thursday (2025-07-10). Kick-off benchmark run week of July 14. POC timeline 3-4 weeks.
[07:26] Maria Gomez: thanks all. That works.
[07:29] Daniel Park: thanks.
[07:31] Sofia Chen: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with calendar invites and the packet.
[07:35] 
Notes: transcription has minor mis-hears (K V cash / KV cache sometimes transcribed as K V cash), some proper nouns normalized. References to shared artifacts: "pricing spreadsheet" and "benchmark plan" to be shared as links in follow-up.
